title: “THE WAGES OF SIN IS DEATH”—BUT WHY DO WE KEEP STOPPING BEFORE THE WORDS THAT COULD SAVE SOMEONE’S LIFE?
paragraphs: “THE WAGES OF SIN IS DEATH”—BUT WHY DO WE KEEP STOPPING BEFORE THE WORDS THAT COULD SAVE SOMEONE’S LIFE?

We have quoted the sentence that condemns us so often that some people have never heard the sentence that reveals the heart of God. Romans 6:23 was never meant to leave a sinner standing at the grave when Jesus Christ has already opened the door to eternal life.
There is something deeply heartbreaking about hearing a person quote half a Bible verse with absolute confidence while leaving out the very words that reveal the hope of the Gospel.
“The wages of sin is death.”
And then silence.

The preacher closes his Bible. The congregation grows quiet. Someone in the back row lowers his head because he knows exactly what he did last night. A woman who has been secretly fighting the same sin for years feels another wave of shame wash over her. A young believer who already wonders whether God has given up on him hears the word death echoing inside his chest.
And nobody finishes the verse.
Nobody tells them about the gift.
Nobody tells them about the Savior.
Nobody tells them that the very same sentence announcing what sin deserves also announces what God freely gives through Jesus Christ.
Imagine walking into a hospital, hearing a doctor announce that you have a deadly disease, and then watching him walk away without telling you that treatment is available.
The diagnosis may be completely accurate.
But the conversation is tragically unfinished.
And somewhere in our churches, our comment sections, our evangelistic conversations, and our social media posts, we have sometimes done something similar with Romans 6:23.
We have preached the wages.
But we have failed to proclaim the gift.
And before anyone misunderstands, this is not an argument for making sin sound less serious.
Sin is deadly.
Judgment is real.
Repentance is necessary.
The holiness of God is not negotiable.
But neither is the grace of God a footnote.
Because the apostle Paul did not write Romans 6:23 to make people stare at death without seeing Jesus.
He wrote:
“For the wages of sin is death; but the gift of God is eternal life through Jesus Christ our Lord.” — Romans 6:23, KJV
Read that again.
Slowly.
Especially the word that stands between death and life.
BUT.
That little word is carrying an announcement bigger than the grave.
Sin pays death.
But God gives life.
And if you have ever felt like your failures have spoken the final word over your existence, you need to hear what comes after that but.
Because your sin may explain why you desperately need a Savior.
But your sin does not have the authority to cancel what Jesus Christ accomplished at Calvary.
There is a difference between exposing someone's sin and proclaiming the Gospel that calls that sinner to repentance and faith.
One tells the truth about the wound.
The other also reveals the One who can heal it.
And Christianity without the finished work of Jesus Christ is not the Gospel Paul preached.
It is a diagnosis without the announcement of the cure.
Now, before we go further, we need to return to the actual words Paul wrote.
Not because Greek automatically makes a sermon more powerful.
Not because knowing ancient languages makes someone more spiritual.
But because Scripture deserves more than emotional slogans detached from their meaning.
Romans 6:23 was originally written in Koine Greek, not Hebrew or Aramaic.
The Greek text reads:
τὰ γὰρ ὀψώνια τῆς ἁμαρτίας θάνατος, τὸ δὲ χάρισμα τοῦ θεοῦ ζωὴ αἰώνιος ἐν Χριστῷ Ἰησοῦ τῷ κυρίῳ ἡμῶν.
A careful English rendering is:
“For the wages of sin are death, but the gracious gift of God is eternal life in Christ Jesus our Lord.”
Notice the contrast Paul deliberately constructs.
The Greek word translated “wages” is ὀψώνια (opsōnia).
It refers to pay, compensation, or provisions received for service, and was also used for a soldier's pay.
In Romans 6, where Paul has been describing slavery to sin and obedience to God, that language becomes devastatingly appropriate.
Sin is not a harmless employer.
It promises freedom while producing bondage.
It offers pleasure while concealing destruction.
It persuades people to surrender their lives in exchange for things that cannot save them.
And when Paul announces that sin pays death, he is exposing the terrible outcome of serving a master that cannot give life.
Think about that.
Some people have spent years working for something that is slowly destroying them.
A man sacrifices his marriage for a secret relationship he calls happiness.
A woman builds her identity around approval until she no longer recognizes herself without it.
A young person feeds an addiction that promises relief but leaves deeper emptiness.
A respected church leader hides dishonesty beneath a reputation for holiness.
A believer keeps returning to bitterness because forgiveness feels like surrendering the right to be angry.
Different stories.
Different struggles.
The same terrible deception.
Sin promises more than it can deliver.
And the payment is far worse than the advertisement.

Paul's warning is not merely that sin makes life difficult. Scripture connects sin with death, judgment, and separation from the life of God. Romans 5:12 declares that sin entered the world through one man, and death through sin. Romans 6:21 asks what fruit came from the things of which believers are now ashamed, and answers that their end is death.
This is serious.
Painfully serious.
But something extraordinary happens when Paul reaches the second half of verse 23.
He does not write that the wages of righteousness are eternal life.
He does not say that good people earn heaven through enough religious activity.
He does not announce that God will reward everyone who manages to maintain an impressive spiritual record.
Instead, he changes the entire category.
From wages to gift.
From earning to receiving.
From what sin pays to what God graciously gives.
The Greek word is χάρισμα (charisma).
It means a gracious gift, something freely given as an expression of favor.
And that matters more than we may realize.
Paul could have continued speaking in the language of payment.
But he did not.
Because eternal life is not a salary for religious performance.
It is God's gift in Jesus Christ.
And if eternal life were something we could earn, the cross would not be the glorious announcement of divine grace that the New Testament proclaims.
Ephesians 2:8–9 says:
“For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God: Not of works, lest any man should boast.”
Grace does not mean that sin is harmless.
Grace means that salvation is something sinners could never purchase for themselves.
And this is where the Gospel begins to confront both the openly rebellious person and the secretly self-righteous religious person.
Because one may believe he is too sinful to be saved.
The other may believe he is good enough to save himself.
But both need Jesus.
Both stand before a holy God.
Both must abandon the illusion of self-salvation.
Both are called to repent and believe the Gospel.
And both must understand that eternal life comes through Christ, not through their own deserving.
Can you imagine the thief on the cross hearing only the first half of Romans 6:23?
He knew what guilt looked like.
He had no respectable religious reputation to present.
No years of charitable service to parade before Jesus.
No opportunity to climb down from his cross and rebuild his life.
He was dying beside the only One who could save him.
And in Luke 23:41–42, he acknowledged his own guilt, recognized Jesus' innocence, and pleaded:
“Lord, remember me when thou comest into thy kingdom.”
Jesus did not pretend the man's crimes had never happened.
He did not announce that sin no longer mattered.
He answered the repentant man's appeal with a promise:
“Verily I say unto thee, To day shalt thou be with me in paradise.” — Luke 23:43, KJV
Do you see it?
The thief had no time to accumulate a lifetime of religious accomplishments.
But he was not beyond the reach of the Savior.
The wages of sin were real.
And the gift of God was standing beside him, bearing the suffering of the cross.
That is not cheap grace.
That is astonishing mercy.
And it should humble every person who has ever looked at another sinner and quietly thought, At least I am not that bad.
Because the ground is level at the foot of the cross.
Now think about another person.
Not a criminal dying in public.
But a woman dragged into public humiliation.
John 8 describes a woman brought before Jesus after being caught in adultery. Her accusers wanted to use her situation to test Him.
Imagine the fear.
The shame.
The eyes.
The whispers.
The terrible realization that her worst moment had become a public spectacle.
And Jesus, without denying the seriousness of sin, exposed the hypocrisy of those eager to condemn her.
After her accusers departed, He said:
“Neither do I condemn thee: go, and sin no more.” — John 8:11, KJV
Do not separate those two declarations.
“Neither do I condemn thee.”
“Go, and sin no more.”
Mercy did not become permission.
And holiness did not disappear when mercy arrived.
Jesus neither joined the crowd in crushing her nor encouraged her to remain in the sin that had brought such ruin.
His words held mercy and a call to changed living together.
That is something our generation desperately needs to recover.
Some preach condemnation so relentlessly that wounded people struggle to believe God is merciful.
Others preach acceptance in ways that leave people imagining repentance is unnecessary.
But biblical grace refuses both distortions.
Jesus does not save us by declaring our rebellion harmless.
He saves us from sin's guilt and dominion, calling us into a new life under His lordship.
Romans 6:1–2 makes this unmistakable.
Paul asks whether believers should continue in sin so that grace may abound.
His answer is emphatic:
“God forbid.”
In Greek, the expression is μὴ γένοιτο (mē genoito), a forceful rejection that can be rendered, “Absolutely not!” or “May it never be!”
The same chapter that celebrates the gift of eternal life refuses to turn grace into an excuse for continuing in sin.
This is why we cannot faithfully preach Romans 6:23 by quoting only the frightening half.
But neither can we faithfully preach it by using the comforting half to excuse rebellion.
The entire chapter matters.
Paul has been teaching that believers united with Christ in His death and resurrection are no longer to present themselves as slaves to sin.
Romans 6:11 calls believers to reckon themselves dead to sin and alive to God in Christ Jesus.
Romans 6:14 declares that sin shall not have dominion over them because they are under grace.
Romans 6:22 describes those who have been set free from sin and become servants of God, bearing fruit unto holiness, with eternal life as the end.
Then comes verse 23.
It is not an isolated slogan.
It is the closing contrast of an argument about two masters, two ways of living, and two radically different outcomes.
Sin leads to death.
God gives eternal life in Christ.
And the grace that saves also begins to transform.
This means that when someone truly comes to Jesus, the Gospel does not merely offer a better feeling about an unchanged life.
It calls for a new allegiance.
A new direction.
A new relationship with sin.
A new life in Christ.
Not sinless perfection achieved overnight.
But a real turning toward the Savior, whose grace teaches believers to deny ungodliness, as Titus 2:11–12 explains.
And perhaps this is where the message becomes uncomfortably personal.
Because there are people reading this who know the language of grace but have been secretly negotiating with sin.
You know the verse.
You know the songs.
You know when to say amen.
You know how to appear spiritually strong.
But there is a conversation you keep hiding.
A habit you keep defending.
A bitterness you keep feeding.
A dishonest decision you keep postponing the need to confess.
And somewhere inside, you have begun confusing God's patience with His approval.
Please hear this carefully.
The second half of Romans 6:23 is not God's permission slip for the first half.
The gift of eternal life was never meant to make us comfortable serving the very sin from which Christ came to rescue us.
Romans 2:4 teaches that God's goodness leads us toward repentance.
Not toward spiritual carelessness.
Not toward calculated disobedience.
Toward repentance.
And repentance is not merely feeling bad because consequences have arrived.
The Greek noun μετάνοια (metanoia) refers to repentance, involving a change of mind and a turning away from sin toward God.
Genuine repentance bears fruit in the way we live.
It does not purchase salvation.
It is part of our response to the God who calls us out of darkness and into the light of His Son.
But there is another person reading this who needs to hear something different.
You are not looking for permission to sin.
You are exhausted from fighting it.
You have confessed the same struggle more times than you can count.
You have cried after promising yourself that you would never return to that place.
You love Jesus, but you are painfully aware of how much you still need His sanctifying work.
And every time someone quotes, “The wages of sin is death,” your heart sinks.
Because you already know.
You know sin is terrible.
You know your weakness is real.
You know how easily your heart can wander.
What you need is not a preacher pretending that holiness is optional.
You need someone to open the Bible and remind you that Jesus Christ is a sufficient Savior.
Listen to 1 John 1:9:
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.”
And 1 John 2:1 speaks directly to believers:
“My little children, these things write I unto you, that ye sin not. And if any man sin, we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous.”
Notice that balance again.
“That ye sin not.”
And:
“If any man sin, we have an advocate.”
God's Word does not encourage sin.
But neither does it leave a repentant believer without hope.
The Advocate is Jesus Christ the righteous.
Not your perfect record.
Not your emotional intensity.
Not the number of tears you shed.
Jesus Christ.
His righteousness.
His sacrifice.
His intercession.
And that is why Romans 8:1 announces:
“There is therefore now no condemnation to them which are in Christ Jesus.”
This is not a blanket declaration that unrepentant rebellion carries no consequence.
It is a glorious assurance for those who belong to Christ.
The believer's hope rests not in denying sin but in belonging to the Savior who has dealt with it.
Somebody needs to read that twice.
Because you have spent so long measuring your relationship with God by the emotional intensity of your failures that you have forgotten to look at the sufficiency of your Redeemer.
You should grieve over sin.
You should confess it.
You should turn away from it.
You should seek accountability and practical help where needed.
But do not mistake endless self-condemnation for spiritual maturity.
The cross does not call you to pretend you were never guilty.
It calls you to trust the One who bore the guilt of sinners.
And if you are in Christ, your identity is not finally determined by the worst thing you have ever done.
It is grounded in the Savior to whom you now belong.
This is the scandal of grace.
Not that God overlooks evil.
But that the holy God provides redemption for guilty people through the sacrifice of His own Son.
Romans 3:23–26 explains that all have sinned and fall short of God's glory, and that justification comes by His grace through the redemption found in Christ Jesus.
God does not become unjust in order to forgive.
At the cross, His righteousness and mercy are revealed.
And when we speak about that cross, we must never make it sound like Jesus was an unwilling victim of a Father who stopped loving Him.
The New Testament reveals the united saving purpose of God.
Jesus willingly laid down His life.
John 10:18 records His declaration that no one takes His life from Him, but that He lays it down of Himself.
And Romans 5:8 says:
“But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.”
While we were yet sinners.
Not after we repaired ourselves.
Not after we became spiritually impressive.
Not after we finally developed a flawless testimony.
While we were yet sinners.
Christ died for us.
And this is where the entire message changes.
Because the Gospel does not say that sinners are secretly innocent.
It says that guilty sinners can be forgiven and made new through Jesus Christ.
It does not erase the reality of judgment.
It announces the Savior through whom we may be rescued.
It does not promise that following Jesus will eliminate every earthly consequence of our past decisions.
A broken relationship may require years of rebuilding.
A betrayed spouse may need time to heal.
A crime may still carry legal consequences.
An addiction may require sustained treatment, accountability, and difficult daily choices.
Forgiveness does not automatically remove every consequence.
But God's grace can transform the person who must face those consequences.
And that transformation can begin in places where everyone else has stopped expecting anything good.
Remember Peter.
The disciple who declared that he would never abandon Jesus.
The man who believed his loyalty was stronger than the coming trial.
Then came the courtyard.
The questions.
The fear.
The denial.
And the rooster.
Luke 22:61–62 records that Jesus turned and looked at Peter, and Peter went out and wept bitterly.
Imagine carrying that memory.
The sound of your own voice denying the One you loved.
The terrible realization that you were not as strong as you thought.
And then imagine hearing that Jesus had risen from the dead.
Would Peter dare to hope?
Would he expect rejection?
Would he assume that his failure had permanently disqualified him?
John 21 records the risen Jesus speaking with Peter beside the Sea of Tiberias.
Three times, Jesus questioned Peter about his love.
And Peter, who had denied Him three times, was entrusted with the responsibility of caring for His sheep.
Jesus did not pretend Peter's denial was insignificant.
But Peter's failure was not the end of his story.
Grace met him.
Restoration followed.
And the man who once denied knowing Jesus would later publicly proclaim Him.
That is what makes the Gospel so extraordinary.
The Savior who knows the truth about us is the same Savior who calls us to follow Him.
And maybe that is why this message hurts in the right places.
Because some of us are Peter.
We made promises we did not keep.
We said we would never return to a particular sin.
We said our faith would never become cold.
We said we would stand for Christ even if everyone else walked away.
Then pressure came.
Temptation came.
Fear came.
And we discovered how fragile our own strength could be.
But listen.
Peter's restoration does not mean that betrayal was harmless.
It means Jesus was greater than Peter's failure.
And the same Christ who restored Peter remains mighty to save.
Not because we deserve another opportunity.
But because His grace is real.
That is why we must be careful with the way we speak to struggling people.
Truth without love can be wielded cruelly.
Love without truth can become empty reassurance.
But Jesus Christ is full of grace and truth, as John 1:14 declares.
We do not have to choose between proclaiming God's holiness and announcing His mercy.
We must proclaim both.
And we must proclaim them as Scripture does.
If you tell a sinner only that sin leads to death, you have spoken a biblical truth.
But you have not yet finished the Gospel announcement contained in Romans 6:23.
If you tell someone only that God gives eternal life while refusing to speak about sin, repentance, and the necessity of faith in Christ, you have also distorted the message.
The Gospel is not merely bad news.
And it is not sentimental good news disconnected from our desperate condition.
It is the good news that God has acted in Jesus Christ to save sinners who cannot save themselves.
Christ died for our sins according to the Scriptures.
He was buried.
He rose again on the third day according to the Scriptures.
That is the apostolic proclamation summarized in 1 Corinthians 15:3–4.
The empty tomb matters.
Because Christianity does not end with a dead teacher offering inspiring moral advice.
It proclaims a crucified and risen Lord.
The resurrection is God's triumphant declaration that death does not have the final victory over Christ.
And those who belong to Him have the promise of resurrection life.
Romans 6:23 does not merely say that God gives a temporary emotional improvement.
It says He gives ζωὴ αἰώνιος (zōē aiōnios).
Eternal life.
Life in Christ that begins with knowing God and reaches its fullness in the resurrection and the age to come.
Jesus said in John 17:3:
“And this is life eternal, that they might know thee the only true God, and Jesus Christ, whom thou hast sent.”
Eternal life is not simply an endless extension of our present broken existence.
It is life in relationship with God through His Son, ultimately freed from sin, death, and corruption.
That is the gift.
Not merely escaping punishment.
But being reconciled to God.
Not merely receiving a clean record.
But being brought into a new life with Christ.
Not merely having yesterday forgiven.
But receiving a living hope for eternity.
And suddenly, the contrast in Romans 6:23 becomes almost overwhelming.
Sin offers wages.
God offers a gift.
Sin leads to death.
Christ gives eternal life.
Sin enslaves.
Christ sets free.
Sin produces shame.
Grace brings forgiveness and transformation.
And none of this happened because sin was a small problem.
It happened because Jesus Christ is a great Savior.
Now I want you to think about someone you know.
Not a hypothetical sinner in a sermon illustration.
A real person.
Someone whose name is in your phone.
Someone who has stopped attending church because they believe everyone there remembers their failure.
Someone who smiles in family photographs but privately wonders whether God still wants them.
Someone who is angry at Christianity because all they ever heard was condemnation without an understandable explanation of the Gospel.
Someone who has never opened a Bible because they assume Jesus came only for respectable people.
Someone who thinks repentance is pointless because they have already ruined too much.
What if that person has heard the first half of Romans 6:23 a hundred times but has never understood the second?
What if the words they desperately need are the words we keep leaving out?
“But the gift of God is eternal life through Jesus Christ our Lord.”
That is not a guarantee that every person who reads a verse will immediately believe.
Salvation is the work of God's grace, not the result of a clever emotional technique.
But it is a reason to be faithful with the whole message.
Because we are not called merely to win arguments about sin.
We are called to bear witness to Jesus Christ.
And perhaps the next time you see someone sharing Romans 6:23, you can lovingly encourage them to finish it.
Not to silence the warning.
But to complete the witness.
Not to minimize the seriousness of sin.
But to magnify the sufficiency of Christ.
Not to make people feel comfortable in rebellion.
But to invite them to repentance, faith, and new life.
And if you are reading this as someone who has never surrendered to Jesus, I want to speak directly to you.
You do not have to pretend that your past is clean.
You do not have to invent a religious identity to impress God.
You do not have to wait until you feel worthy of salvation.
You are called to repent and believe in Jesus Christ.
Mark 1:15 records Jesus proclaiming:
“Repent ye, and believe the gospel.”
Come honestly.
Confess your sin.
Turn toward Him.
Trust the crucified and risen Savior.
Do not make peace with the very sin that is destroying you.
And do not believe the lie that your darkness is greater than His power to save.
Jesus said in John 6:37:
“Him that cometh to me I will in no wise cast out.”
What a promise.
Not that everyone who casually admires Jesus has automatically received eternal life.
But that the one who truly comes to Him will not be rejected.
You may have been rejected by people.
You may have disappointed your family.
You may have destroyed opportunities.
You may have spent years building a life around things you now regret.
But the Gospel still calls you to Christ.
And if you already belong to Him, perhaps this is your moment to stop treating grace like a theory and begin living in grateful obedience.
Confess what needs confessing.
Make restitution where it is appropriate and possible.
Seek forgiveness where you have caused harm, without demanding that others immediately trust you again.
Ask for help if your struggle has become more than you can manage alone.
Return to Scripture.
Return to prayer.
Return to fellowship with believers who will speak both truth and grace into your life.
Do not hide behind the language of forgiveness while refusing the work of repentance.
And do not surrender to despair when sanctification proves to be a lifelong battle.
Keep looking to Christ.
Keep walking in the light.
Keep trusting the grace that saves and teaches.
Because the point of Romans 6:23 is not that death is imaginary.
It is that eternal life is genuinely offered in Jesus Christ.
And that changes everything.
This is also why Gospel Warrior exists.
Not to build a community around one personality.
Not to replace the local church.
Not to sell the idea that spiritual growth can be purchased.
But to keep placing the Word of God before people who need to hear it.
People who are searching.
People who are struggling.
People who have been wounded.
People who have grown spiritually cold.
People who are beginning again.
People who need to be reminded that repentance and grace belong together.
Those resources are part of a larger mission: helping people read Scripture, understand the Gospel, grow in discernment, and follow Christ with greater faithfulness.
And if this article has strengthened you, challenged you, or helped you understand God's Word more clearly, I want to invite you to become part of sustaining that mission.
It is not a purchase of forgiveness.
It is not a condition for being a faithful Christian.
Scripture teaches in 2 Corinthians 9:7:
“Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.”
That matters.
Because Gospel ministry should never manipulate people into giving from fear, guilt, or the belief that salvation depends on financial support.
But neither should we overlook the beautiful opportunity to participate in the work of spreading biblical truth.
These are simply expressions of appreciation.
The greatest gift we can proclaim is not a product, a discount, or membership in an online community.
It is Jesus Christ.
And that Gospel remains free to hear, believe, and share.
Read.
Grow.
Pray.
Share the truth.
Keep seeking Christ.
Your financial circumstances do not determine your worth before God or your place among those who sincerely desire to follow Him.
Not simply because we want another post to circulate.
But because there may be someone among your friends who has heard about sin for years without understanding the grace offered in Jesus Christ.
Someone you would never think to approach with a long theological conversation.
Someone who is quietly questioning whether their life can change.
Someone who needs to know that Romans 6:23 does not end at death.
Send this privately to someone you love.
Invite your family, your friends, the struggling believer, the spiritually indifferent, the seeker, and even the person who does not yet believe to come and examine the truth of God's Word with us.
And please, do not leave this conversation without reflecting on what God may be showing you.
Or share, in your own words, how Jesus has changed your understanding of repentance and forgiveness.

You do not need to reveal private details or confess sensitive matters in a public comment section. God hears the prayers you never post, and trusted pastoral care is a better place for struggles requiring privacy.
But let the conversation point to Christ.
Let testimonies strengthen others.
Let honest questions be welcomed.
Let those who are struggling discover that they are not the only ones seeking to walk faithfully with Jesus.
Because one of the most beautiful things a Christian community can do is remind one another of the entire counsel of God.
Not just the warnings we find easiest to repeat.
Not just the promises we find most comforting.
The whole truth.
The holiness that exposes sin.
The mercy that welcomes repentant sinners.
The cross that reveals the cost of redemption.
The resurrection that announces Christ's victory.
The grace that saves.
The Spirit who sanctifies.
The hope of eternal life.
And above all, the Lord Jesus Christ Himself.
So the next time you hear someone declare, “The wages of sin is death,” do not rush to argue with them.
That statement is true.
Let it stand with all the seriousness Paul intended.
But do not let the sentence die there.
Finish the verse.
Finish the announcement.
Tell the truth about sin.
And then tell the truth about the Savior.
Because somewhere, a person who has spent years believing that their worst failure is the end of their story may finally hear the words they never knew came next.
“But the gift of God is eternal life through Jesus Christ our Lord.”
Not eternal life through religious popularity.
Not eternal life through perfect attendance.
Not eternal life through charitable giving.
Not eternal life through the ability to hide every weakness.
Eternal life through Jesus Christ our Lord.
That is the center.
That is the hope.
That is the Gospel.
And if there is one thing I want you to remember long after you close this article, it is this:
God did not reveal the terrible wages of sin so that we would ignore the gracious gift He offers in His Son.
He told us the truth about death.
And then He pointed us to Jesus Christ, who died for sinners and rose again.
The cross is where the seriousness of our sin and the greatness of God's saving love confront us together.
The empty tomb is where our hope rests upon the victory of the risen Lord.
And Romans 6:23 is where one unforgettable contrast reminds us that what sin earns and what God gives are not the same thing.
So preach the warning.
Call people to repentance.
Never dilute holiness.
Never turn grace into permission for rebellion.
But for the sake of faithfulness to Scripture, do not stop before the gift.
Because the tragedy is not only that sin pays in death. It is that someone might walk away believing death is the final word, when the verse was pointing them to Jesus all along.
